vignette:
Gerald Howarth is a 68-year-old married politician of European descent who has spent the better part of four decades in public life, accustomed to scrutiny and the performance of composure. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after a life-threatening road traffic accident that he has struggled, in his own words, to "put behind him the way a man of my experience should be able to."

The accident occurred on a wet November evening when Gerald was being driven home from a late legislative session. His driver, who Gerald later learned had consumed alcohol before the journey, lost control of the vehicle on a highway interchange. The car was struck broadside by a lorry, spun across two lanes, and came to rest against a concrete barrier. Gerald sustained fractured ribs, a collapsed lung, and lacerations to his face and left arm. He was conscious throughout, pinned against the crumpled door, aware of the smell of alcohol emanating from the driver and of the particular silence that descended after the impact - a silence that preceded the sound of approaching sirens by what felt to him like an eternity. He remembers the event not as a continuous sequence but as a series of frozen images: the headlights of the lorry filling the window, the driver's hands leaving the wheel, the angle of the crushed metal against his chest. He has found, in the months since, that when he attempts to recount the accident - to his wife, to colleagues who have asked - he loses the thread somewhere in the middle, the words dissolving before he can reach the end, leaving him staring at whoever is listening with a sentence unfinished.

In the weeks following his discharge from hospital, Gerald noticed that the smell of alcohol - at receptions, at the parliamentary bar, at the dinner table when wine was poured - produced an immediate and overwhelming wave of discomfort that he could not rationalise away. He began declining evening events where drinking was likely, offering scheduling conflicts as the reason. He also stopped travelling by car entirely. This was not a minor inconvenience for a working politician. His constituency is rural, his diary demanding. He began arriving late to votes, missing engagements he had previously considered non-negotiable, and delegating travel to junior staff under the pretence of workload. His chief of staff has quietly noted the change. Gerald is aware that colleagues have begun to talk, and this awareness compounds something he has come to believe with a conviction that surprises even him: that people can look at him now and see what happened, that the accident is somehow visible on him, legible in his face or his bearing. In committee rooms and on the floor of the chamber, he has found concentration increasingly difficult to sustain, his attention drifting mid-debate in ways that would once have been unthinkable.

At night, Gerald wakes repeatedly, often rising to check that the house is locked, that his wife is breathing, that nothing is wrong - unable to articulate what he is checking for, only that the waking feels necessary. Unusual quiet - the absence of traffic, a lull in conversation - produces in him a specific and visceral dread, as though silence itself has become a harbinger. When the memories return, they are accompanied by a physical sensation of pressure across his chest and pain along the left side of his ribcage, the body apparently rehearsing what the mind cannot finish.

What has weighed on Gerald most persistently is a form of self-recrimination he cannot seem to reason his way out of. He dwells repeatedly on the fact that he chose that driver, that he had ignored a prior complaint about the man's reliability, that he had been in a hurry. He has come to believe, with a quiet but immovable certainty, that the accident happened because of the kind of man he is - someone who prioritises efficiency over care, whose judgment cannot be trusted. This belief sits beneath his public life like a fault line.

Gerald sought help only after his wife told him she was frightened - not of him, but for him. What he most fears, sitting in the consulting room, is that speaking about it will confirm what he already suspects about himself. What he most hopes is that it will not.
